q: According to the book's analysis, which cost driver accounts for the largest share of API spend?
options: Heartbeats and background tasks
Improper model selection
Context accumulation from resending full conversation history
Multi-round reasoning on complex tasks
explanation: The six-driver table puts context accumulation at 40–50% of spend, well above the other drivers. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.1)

q: After routing heartbeats to tinyllama, heartbeat responses become erratic on a workspace with large memory logs. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: Its 2,048-token context is too small; switch to a larger local model such as qwen2.5:7b.
Ollama is rate-limiting requests; raise the heartbeat interval.
tinyllama lacks tool support; route heartbeats back to Sonnet.
The cache TTL expired; raise cacheControlTtl.
explanation: The book names the small context window as tinyllama's failure mode and suggests phi-4 or qwen2.5:7b, both still free via Ollama. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.2)

q: Why does the book recommend static routing over dynamic routing for most deployments?
options: It always produces lower cost than dynamic routing.
Dynamic routing is not supported by OpenClaw.
Static routing sends every request to Haiku.
It needs no classification logic and cannot misfire.
explanation: Static routing is less theoretically optimal but simpler: the user or AGENTS.md picks the profile, so nothing can misclassify. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.3)

q: A SOUL.md says to use the best available model for anything important to the user. What effect does the book predict?
options: The router ignores identity files, so there is no effect.
Most requests get classified as important, skewing routing toward the premium model.
Requests are split evenly across tiers.
The agent refuses to use Haiku for any task.
explanation: The book warns that identity-file wording like this drives tier inflation and says to audit identity files for implicit model instructions. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.3)

q: In every session, the second turn logs cache_hit_tokens as 0. The session init code prepends the current timestamp to the context. What is happening?
options: The TTL is too long, so the cache never refreshes.
Haiku does not support prompt caching.
Cache reads are only logged on turn 3 and later.
Variable content before the stable prefix breaks the byte match, so the cache never hits.
explanation: Any variable content placed ahead of the stable prefix invalidates the whole cache. Keep stable content first and variable content last. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.5.5)

q: A user messages the agent about once an hour throughout the day. Which cacheControlTtl does the book recommend?
options: 300 seconds
3600 seconds
60 seconds
604800 seconds
explanation: For periodic hourly use the book recommends a one-hour TTL so the cache stays warm across gaps. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.5.2)

q: When is prompt caching likely to cost more than it saves?
options: A single, one-off Opus call whose prefix is not reused within the TTL
An interactive chat with several turns in five minutes
A high-frequency Haiku pipeline
A batch job that reuses the same prefix nightly with a 24-hour TTL
explanation: The 25% write premium is only recovered by later reads. A single-use call pays the premium with no reads to offset it. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.5.6)

q: Which budget action does the book recommend for a monthly limit, and why?
options: pause, so the agent resumes at midnight
warn, so processing is never interrupted
disable, so the agent stays stopped until someone investigates
pause, so queued messages are dropped
explanation: Disable needs a manual re-enable, giving you a chance to look into the cause before the agent runs again. Pause fits daily limits. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.6)

q: A cron typo schedules a task at a 5-minute interval when 5 hours was intended. What role do budget controls play?
options: They prevent the cron job from being scheduled.
They catch the runaway within the first day instead of at month end.
They have no effect because cron tasks bypass budgets.
They automatically correct the cron expression.
explanation: The book lists runaway automation as a tail scenario that daily limits catch quickly, before it compounds over the billing cycle. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.6)

q: In the book's month-one optimization trajectory, which change comes first?
options: Enabling tiered model routing
Configuring session pruning
Adding multi-provider routing through OpenRouter
Routing heartbeats to a local Ollama model
explanation: Day 1 is heartbeat routing: quick to set up, immediate effect, no capability change. Routing and pruning come in later weeks. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §6.8)
